newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kok doesn't rule out special EU summit on reform.
newsitem.headline: Kok doesn't rule out special EU summit on reform.

text.p: Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said on Wednesday he did not rule out the possibility of an informal European Union summit in May to speed up negotiations on reforming EU institutions after the British elections.

Kok told reporters after talks with French President Jacques Chirac that his government, which holds the six-month rotating EU presidency, would propose draft texts on key issues in the EU's Inter-Governmental Conference (IGC) later this month.

"Then we will see what the reaction is, we are preparing a draft treaty for mid-May. Depending on the result of the British elections, we could envisage (an informal summit) but for the moment there is no precise timetable," he said.

"We are naturally not ruling out the possibility of having a special council (summit), if there is a need. But to announce an informal summit without a clear objective would not be productive," he said.
French presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said the essential objective was to achieve a substantial agreement on reform at the next regular EU summit in Amsterdam in June.

Diplomats said it was premature to trumpet a decisive summit for after the British general elections, since it could play into the hands of Euro-sceptics in Britain who wanted to block any further EU integration.

Officials in Brussels said on Tuesday Christian Democratic leaders discussed holding a special summit after Britain's elections to see what a new government in London might be willing to accept in a new EU treaty.

Kok said he had held long, detailed discussions with Chirac on the major issues of EU reform, including French proposals for reducing the size of the European Commission, a stronger foreign and security policy and a bigger role for national parliaments.
He reported that Chirac had pressed for the IGC to bar the European Parliament from dealing with issues which were the domain of national governments and parliaments.
France clashed with the Strasbourg-based assembly last week after it passed a resolution urging Paris to withdraw a controversial bill to clamp down on illegal immigration.

Officials said France was now proposing that each EU member state should nominate a single European Commissioner, but that not all would be full members of the Commission for the full duration of their mandate. The roles of senior and junior commissioners would be allocated by the Commission president.
